newsitem.title: TURKEY: IMF warns Turkey on weakness in public finances.
newsitem.headline: IMF warns Turkey on weakness in public finances.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund warned Turkey on Thursday of its need to address serious public finance imbalances, prompting Ankara to detail plans for a medium-term programme aimed at fighting chronic inflation.

"The fundamental problems of a structural weakness in the public finances remain to be tackled," IMF delegation chief Martin Hardy told reporters at the end of two weeks of talks with the government in Ankara.
Turkey posted a budget defict of $1.3 billion last year and public sector borrowing amounted to around eight percent of gross national product (GNP).
After a meeting with State Minister Ufuk Soylemez, Hardy also cautioned Turkey on its annual inflation rate, which he said was still too high at around 80 percent.
"The inflationary process remains extremely high," he said. Turkey's extension of maturities in domestic borrowing only postponed the country's debt-servicing problems, he added.
Maturities have grown recently to an average of around 13 months from three to four months a year ago.

As expected, the IMF talks with the Islamist-led government did not yield a stand-by agreement, but Soylemez, responsible for the Treasury and privatisation, indicated that Ankara would seek support from international organisations for its future financial plans.

He said a decision had been taken to set up a working team to coordinate a two to three year economic plan aimed at fighting the country's long-term inflation problem. In March, wholesale price inflation rose 77 percent year-on-year.
The team, coordinated by the Treasury, will involve the State Planning Institute, Finance Ministry, Privatisation Administration and Central Bank, Soylemez said.

"We believe we will have taken an important step in Turkey's efforts to tackle structural reforms, primarily the struggle against inflation...if the support of international credit is obtained for this programme," he said.
He added that the framework of the programme was aimed at being completed by September.
Hardy said one of the priorities of the government should be to tackle the problems of the costly social security system, reform of which has been on the agenda for several years.
"In the meantime the deficit of the social security system has been increasing very rapidly and has eroded the basic fiscal position," Hardy said.

According to labour ministry figures, the country's social security institution is expected to post a deficit of 321 trillion lira ($2.4 billion) in 1997. Economists have forecast that it could have a debt of $10 billion by the year 2000.
Economists have also cast considerable doubt on the government's target of achieving a balanced budget in 1997 with the help of considerable privatisation income and other revenue raising plans.

Soylemez declined to respond to an earlier reported comment by Hardy that Turkey's budget cash positon showed a deficit of 415 trillion lira in the first quarter. Previously, government ministers have said the budget remained balanced in the early part of the year.
"Turkey is determined in its target of a balanced budget. It is doing all it can to achieve this," Soylemez said.

He said there was already evidence of economic improvements over the last year. He cited falling interest rates, lengthening debt maturities and advances in privatisation, including the programme's centrepiece, Turk Telekom.
